title: CSCI 2122 · Assignment 2 Recall Lab
description: A separate, assignment-scoped recall bank: retrieve one rule, rebuild its syntax, trace interacting concepts, then write small decoder helpers without looking. Reveal the model only after committing an answer; treat a hint-assisted answer as more practice, not independent recall.
assumptions: C17 practice model: 8-bit bytes; 32-bit int and unsigned int; sizeof(int) = 4; two’s-complement signed integers; long long can represent 2^31.
Unless a prompt tests failure or bounds, pointers and buffers are valid, requested fields fit, numeric input is representable, and operations explicitly stated to succeed do succeed.
Relevant standard headers are included. Size and position calculations are representable unless the prompt asks you to check them. Stream positions and array indices are zero-based.

sources.title: CSCI 2122 Assignment 2.pdf
sources.detail: Primary scope. Page 2: input counts, 5-bit length prefix, MSB-first order, Problem 1 constraints/output and examples. Page 3: Problem 2 multiple fields and termination. Page 4 recommends small helper functions and C library functions.

sources.title: WALKTHROUGH.md
sources.detail: Supplementary helper-based explanation, especially §§3–4 and 7. Corrected here where needed: safe L = 31 subtraction, no fixed 16-byte Problem 2 guarantee, zero is nonnegative, and memset does not validate reads or remove padding written afterward.

sources.title: WG14 N1570 C draft
sources.detail: Primary-language reference for supporting rules unchanged in C17: integer promotions, arrays/pointers, sizeof, shifts, scanf/printf, calloc/malloc/free and memset. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

topics.title: 01 · Read the encoding contract
topics.description: Separate input counts, header width, stream order and the two problem variants.
notes: Each field has a five-bit unsigned length L followed by L signed bits.
Problem 1 has B = 0..5; an empty line prints nothing, and unused trailing bits are ignored.
Problem 2 allows more than five bytes without stating a fixed maximum B. Its termination rules are practiced in topic 10.

topics.title: 02 · Recall exact I/O syntax
topics.description: Retrieve conversion tokens, argument types, addresses and output order.
notes: scanf("%d", &n) requires int *; scanf("%x", &temp) requires unsigned int *.
Read each byte into an unsigned int temporary, then store a successfully read value in unsigned-char storage.
printf receives values in conversion order; scanf receives destination addresses.

topics.title: 03 · Distinguish arrays and pointer layers
topics.description: Tell the byte object, its pointer and the address of that pointer apart.
notes: p, *p and &p have different types and meanings.
An array object cannot be assigned; its individual elements can. A pointer assignment copies an address.
sizeof a real array measures the whole array. An array function parameter is adjusted to a pointer, so pass its length separately.

topics.title: 04 · Count bytes and allocate buffers
topics.description: Distinguish element count, element size, capacity, received length and initialization.
notes: calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes and initializes their bits to zero; malloc does not initialize storage.
memset writes a byte value into a specified number of bytes. Clearing storage does not make invalid reads safe.
A buffer must hold B received bytes. Decode only those B bytes, regardless of spare allocated capacity. Check allocation success before use and release dynamic storage with free when finished.

topics.title: 05 · Retrieve masks and bit operators
topics.description: Memorize the small operations before combining them with stream positions.
notes: 1u << k selects bit k for 0 <= k < 32 in this practice model.
Use OR to set, AND with an inverted mask to clear, and XOR to toggle.
Bitwise & and logical && are different operations.

topics.title: 06 · Predict shift behavior precisely
topics.description: Recall the unsigned rules and distinguish invalid counts from valid shifts.
notes: The shift count must be nonnegative and less than the promoted left operand’s width.
Use unsigned operands for bit masks. Signed 32-bit 1 << 31 has undefined behavior.
unsigned char promotes to nonnegative int in the practice model; plain char may be signed.

topics.title: 07 · Locate one MSB-first stream bit
topics.description: Translate a global position into the correct byte and right-shift count.
notes: byteIndex = p / 8; offset = p % 8; shift = 7 - offset.
The bit value is (data[p / 8] >> (7 - p % 8)) & 1u.
B received bytes provide valid positions 0 through 8B - 1, if B is nonzero.

topics.title: 08 · Accumulate a field in order
topics.description: Combine single-bit access, left shifts and a moving bit position.
notes: Start value at zero; append each next bit with value = (value << 1) | bit.
Read a field in increasing global positions even when it crosses byte boundaries.
A field beginning at p consumes 5 + L bits including its header; no byte alignment is inserted.

topics.title: 09 · Decode L-bit two’s complement
topics.description: Separate raw unsigned extraction from width-dependent signed interpretation.
notes: For 1 <= L <= 31, the sign bit is bit L - 1 of raw.
If that bit is clear, the value is raw, including zero. Otherwise the mathematical value is raw - 2^L.
A safe negative branch is (int)((long long)raw - (1LL << L)); do not use signed 32-bit 1 << 31.

topics.title: 10 · Stop and advance at exact boundaries
topics.description: Track remaining bits, payload completeness and per-line counters.
notes: Problem 2 stops when fewer than six bits remain or a header gives L = 0.
After checking pos <= totalBits, use L <= totalBits - pos to confirm payload capacity.
Reset pos and the integer ordinal for each input line. Advance an integer ordinal only after decoding that integer.

topics.title: 11 · Mix the concepts in real streams
topics.description: Trace input bytes through extraction, signed interpretation and output sequencing.
notes: Trace in the order header → width → raw payload → signed value → new cursor.
Write intermediate positions and widths before checking the final number.
Use the PDF examples as checks; then reconstruct the rule on a changed example rather than memorizing one output.

topics.title: 12 · Rebuild small methods from memory
topics.description: Write complete helpers from explicit contracts and check every boundary.
notes: Start from the contract and list the preconditions, result and failure behavior before writing code.
Helper tasks have explicit bounds and status conventions; these are practice contracts, not additional assignment requirements.
Self-mark code against every rubric point, including boundary cases. The exercises deliberately avoid presenting a completed assignment main.

questions.prompt: In the input format, which symbol denotes the number of input lines: N or B?
questions.answer: N
questions.hint: One count belongs to the whole communication.
questions.explanation: N counts input lines. Each following line begins with its own byte count B.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: A line begins `3 0x62 0x69 0x00`. Which input symbol is represented by the leading 3: N or B?
questions.answer: B
questions.hint: This count belongs to one line.
questions.explanation: B is the number of hexadecimal bytes that follow on this input line.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: How many bits encode the length L before each integer?
questions.hint: This header has a fixed width.
questions.explanation: Every field begins with a 5-bit unsigned length, followed by L payload bits.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: An integer has a 12-bit payload. Including its length header, how many stream bits does this field consume?
questions.hint: Header bits plus payload bits.
questions.explanation: The field consumes 5 + L = 5 + 12 = 17 bits; it need not end at a byte boundary.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: What is the largest unsigned length representable by the 5-bit header?
questions.hint: A k-bit unsigned field has maximum 2^k − 1.
questions.explanation: Five header bits encode 0 through 31. A nonzero payload width is therefore at most 31.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: The five header bits are `11111`. What payload width L does this encode?
questions.hint: Interpret the header as unsigned binary.
questions.explanation: The header is a length, so 11111 is unsigned 31, not signed −1.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Within each input byte, which end is read first? Answer MSB or LSB.
questions.answer: MSB
questions.hint: Bit 0 of the stream is the leftmost bit of byte 0.
questions.explanation: The most significant bit of data[0] is first; bytes then follow in array order.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Does moving the decoder from a little-endian host to a big-endian host reverse the prescribed stream order? Explain in one sentence.
questions.answer: No. Read bytes in input order and bits MSB first within each byte on either host.
questions.hint: Distinguish the file’s bit order from the host representation of a multi-byte integer.
questions.explanation: Explicit indexing and shifting of each byte implements the protocol without depending on host byte order.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.
rubric: Says the protocol order does not change.
States input byte order and MSB-first order within each byte.

questions.prompt: For Problem 1, B is 0. How many integers should this input line produce?
questions.hint: No bytes means no header or payload.
questions.explanation: The specification explicitly says a zero-byte line has no integers to unpack.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: The first input line has B = 0 and the second contains one encoded integer. What line number must appear on that integer’s output?
questions.hint: Input line numbers count empty input lines too.
questions.explanation: Line numbering tracks the input stream lines, not the number of previously printed integers.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Is a fixed 16-byte buffer guaranteed sufficient for every valid Problem 2 line by the assignment specification? State why.
questions.answer: No. Problem 2 permits more than 5 bytes and gives no fixed upper bound for B; buffer capacity must accommodate the actual B.
questions.hint: A largest sample is not a maximum input size.
questions.explanation: The walkthrough’s 16-byte suggestion is not a bound stated by the assignment. Allocate for B or use another explicitly capacity-safe strategy.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.
rubric: Says no fixed 16-byte guarantee exists.
Requires capacity for the actual byte count.

questions.prompt: A Problem 2 sample uses 9 bytes. What bound can you infer for all future inputs from that sample alone?
questions.answer: No maximum B can be inferred from one sample; the implementation must support the specified input size rather than assume 9 or 16 bytes.
questions.hint: Examples demonstrate cases, not an unstated limit.
questions.explanation: Problem 1 explicitly bounds B by 5; Problem 2 removes that small bound without supplying a replacement.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.
rubric: Does not invent a 9- or 16-byte maximum.
Distinguishes sample size from a specified input bound.

questions.prompt: Fill the format token to read one decimal value into `int B`: `scanf("___", &B);`
questions.answer: %d
questions.hint: The destination is an int, and the input is decimal.
questions.explanation: scanf %d expects a pointer to int, so &B is the correct destination argument.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Which conversion token belongs in `scanf` for the initial decimal line count `int N`?
questions.answer: %d
questions.hint: Use the signed decimal integer conversion.
questions.explanation: The input’s initial count is decimal. The corresponding destination must be int *.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Fill the format token: `unsigned int temp; scanf("___", &temp);` reads a hexadecimal byte token such as `0xca`.
questions.answer: %x
questions.hint: Hexadecimal without a length modifier.
questions.explanation: scanf %x reads a hexadecimal integer into unsigned int *. It accepts the optional 0x prefix.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: A token is `ff` rather than `0xff`. Which scanf conversion reads it as hexadecimal into unsigned int?
questions.answer: %x
questions.hint: The 0x prefix is optional for this conversion.
questions.explanation: %x accepts both forms. The conversion and destination type must agree.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: With the unmodified `%x` conversion, what exact C type must `temp` have in `scanf("%x", &temp)`?
questions.answer: unsigned int
questions.hint: Do not confuse a byte’s value range with scanf’s destination type.
questions.explanation: Unmodified %x requires unsigned int *. &temp has that type when temp is unsigned int.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Repair this read while keeping `%x` and the unsigned-char buffer. Assume the token is in 0..255.
questions.hint: Read using the required destination type, then store the byte.
questions.explanation: Passing unsigned char * to unmodified %x is a type mismatch; a cast of that pointer is not a repair. An unsigned-int temporary provides the required object.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Reads with unsigned int temp and &temp.
Checks the conversion result before using temp.
Stores temp into data[i] after a successful read.

questions.prompt: Why does reading `int B` use `scanf("%d", &B)` while printing it uses `printf("%d", B)`?
questions.answer: scanf needs B’s address to store a new int in B; printf needs the int value to display.
questions.hint: One operation writes into an object; the other consumes its value.
questions.explanation: C passes each argument by value. For scanf that value is a pointer; for printf %d it is an int.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Explains that scanf receives a destination address.
Explains that printf %d receives the integer value.

questions.prompt: Identify and fix the wrong argument in each line. Assume `B` has already been initialized.
questions.answer:
scanf("%d", &B);
printf("%d", B);
questions.hint: Match each conversion’s expected argument type.
questions.explanation: scanf %d expects int *, while printf %d expects int. Swapping values and addresses violates those contracts.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Adds & for scanf.
Removes & for printf.

questions.prompt: What return value from `scanf("%x", &temp)` means its one requested conversion succeeded?
questions.hint: scanf counts successful assignments.
questions.explanation: One successful conversion gives 1. Do not use temp unless that read succeeded.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: `scanf("%d %x", &B, &temp)` successfully reads B but fails to convert the second token. What does it return?
questions.hint: Count assignments actually completed.
questions.explanation: The first conversion assigned one object; the second failed, so the return value is 1. EOF before any conversion is a different case.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Write the required printf call using `int line`, `int ordinal`, and `int value`, in that order. Include the trailing newline.
questions.answer: printf("Line %d, integer %d: %d\n", line, ordinal, value);
questions.hint: The words, punctuation and argument order are part of the output contract.
questions.explanation: Each %d consumes the next int argument. The first number identifies the input line; the second is the integer’s order within that line.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples. Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Uses exactly Line, comma, integer, colon and spaces as specified.
Supplies line, ordinal, value in that order.
Terminates the output line with \n.

questions.prompt: What exact output line does this call produce?
questions.answer: Line 2, integer 4: -7
questions.hint: Match conversions to arguments from left to right.
questions.explanation: The first argument after the format fills the first %d; variable names do not change that rule.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
questions.code:
int line = 4, ordinal = 2, value = -7;
printf("Line %d, integer %d: %d\n", ordinal, line, value);
rubric: Gives Line 2, integer 4: -7 with the required punctuation.

questions.prompt: Given `unsigned char *p`, what is the type of the expression `*p`?
questions.answer: unsigned char
questions.hint: One dereference removes one pointer layer.
questions.explanation: p is a pointer to unsigned char; *p designates the unsigned-char object to which it points.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.

questions.prompt: Given `unsigned char *p`, what is the type of the expression `&p`?
questions.answer: unsigned char **
questions.hint: Address-of adds a pointer layer to the variable’s own type.
questions.explanation: p is itself a pointer object. &p points to that pointer object, so its type is unsigned char **.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in x after these statements?
questions.hint: &data[1] points to the second element; * reads that element.
questions.explanation: data[1] is 0xca, which is 202. Dereferencing p reads the pointed-to byte.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in data[0] after these statements?
questions.hint: Two dereferences reach the byte through the pointer object.
questions.explanation: pp points to p; *pp is p; **pp designates data[0]. The assignment therefore writes 8 into that byte.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.

questions.prompt: Which assignments are valid C, and what does each valid one change?
questions.answer: p = other is valid and redirects p. data[0] = 7 is valid and changes one byte. data = other is invalid because an array is not an assignable object.
questions.hint: Separate an array object, a pointer variable and one array element.
questions.explanation: In most expressions the array name converts to a pointer to its first element, but the array itself cannot be assigned another array or pointer.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Accepts p = other.
Accepts data[0] = 7.
Rejects data = other rather than claiming it copies bytes.

questions.prompt: Does `p = data` copy five bytes? Explain what it stores.
questions.answer: No. It stores the address of data[0] in p; p then refers to the same array storage.
questions.hint: Pointer assignment copies an address value.
questions.explanation: No new array is created and no elements are copied. Writing p[0] subsequently changes data[0] while p points there.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Says no element copy occurs.
Identifies the address of the first array element.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does `sizeof data` have here?
questions.hint: sizeof measures bytes of the actual array object.
questions.explanation: An unsigned char occupies one C byte. This real array has five such elements.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
questions.code: unsigned char data[5];

questions.prompt: What is `sizeof values / sizeof values[0]` here?
questions.hint: Total array bytes divided by one element’s bytes.
questions.explanation: The expression is the element count, 6. Under the practice assumptions sizeof values is 24, not 6.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
questions.code: int values[6];

questions.prompt: Inside this function, does `sizeof data` measure five bytes of array storage? State what it measures.
questions.answer: No. An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter, so sizeof data is sizeof(unsigned char *).
questions.hint: The brackets in a parameter declaration do not preserve an array object.
questions.explanation: Pass the byte count separately. The parameter’s sizeof cannot recover the caller’s array length; pointer size is not assumed here.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Identifies data as a pointer parameter.
Says sizeof measures the pointer, not the supplied array length.

questions.prompt: Why is this function unable to obtain the input byte count reliably? Give a signature that fixes the missing information.
questions.answer: data is a pointer parameter, so sizeof data is pointer size. Pass the count explicitly, for example void decode(const unsigned char *data, size_t B).
questions.hint: An array argument does not carry its length into the function.
questions.explanation: The count is needed for stream bounds. Using const also documents that the decoder reads the bytes without modifying them.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Rejects sizeof data as the buffer length.
Supplies an explicit length/count parameter.

questions.prompt: After the call, where does caller p point, and what are data[0] and data[1]?
questions.answer: p still points to data[0]; data[0] is 0 and data[1] is 7.
questions.hint: The function receives a copy of the pointer, but both copies refer to shared storage.
questions.explanation: Incrementing local p does not change the caller’s pointer. Dereferencing that local pointer after incrementing changes the second byte.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Caller p still points to data[0].
Gives data[0] = 0 and data[1] = 7.

questions.prompt: After this call, where does caller p point? Explain the pointer layers.
questions.answer: p points to data[1]. pp points to the caller’s pointer object; *pp is that pointer, so incrementing *pp updates caller p.
questions.hint: This time the function receives the address of the pointer variable.
questions.explanation: A pointer-to-pointer can change which byte the caller’s pointer refers to. No byte value is modified by this increment.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Identifies data[1] as the new target.
Explains that *pp designates the caller’s pointer.

questions.prompt: `calloc(4, 2)` succeeds. How many total bytes are allocated?
questions.hint: First argument counts elements; second gives bytes per element.
questions.explanation: calloc allocates 4 elements of 2 bytes each: 4 × 2 = 8 bytes. It does not attach an array length to the returned pointer.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: In `calloc(4, 2)`, which argument is the element count? Answer its numeric value.
questions.hint: Read the signature as calloc(count, element_size).
questions.explanation: The count argument is 4 and the element-size argument is 2 bytes. Swapping them happens to preserve this product but changes their roles.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: The call succeeds. How many int objects fit in this allocation under the practice assumptions?
questions.hint: Divide allocated bytes by sizeof(int).
questions.explanation: calloc(4, 2) reserves 8 bytes, and each int occupies 4 bytes here. The call’s count of 4 does not make it room for four int objects.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code: int *p = calloc(4, 2);

questions.prompt: The call succeeds. How many total bytes does it reserve under the practice assumptions?
questions.hint: sizeof *p measures one int object.
questions.explanation: The idiom allocates six objects of the pointed-to type: 6 × 4 = 24 bytes.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code: int *p = calloc(6, sizeof *p);

questions.prompt: Which function guarantees its successfully allocated bytes are initially all-bits-zero: malloc or calloc?
questions.answer: calloc
questions.hint: The allocation and initialization contracts differ.
questions.explanation: calloc initializes all allocated bits to zero. For unsigned char bytes that gives the numeric value zero.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: A successful `malloc(B)` returns a buffer. May the decoder assume its unread bytes contain zero? Explain.
questions.answer: No. malloc does not initialize the allocated storage; only read bytes after their values have been written, and remain within the buffer bounds.
questions.hint: Getting storage and setting its contents are separate actions.
questions.explanation: Even calloc or memset cannot replace checking that an input conversion succeeded or that a stream position is valid.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
rubric: Says malloc does not zero the storage.
Requires initialization before using byte values.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does this call write?
questions.hint: The third argument is a byte count.
questions.explanation: memset writes exactly the first 3 bytes here, not all 5 elements of the array.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code:
unsigned char data[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
memset(data, 0, 3);

questions.prompt: What decimal value is in data[3] afterward?
questions.hint: Indices 0, 1 and 2 are the only bytes filled.
questions.explanation: The byte at index 3 is outside the three-byte fill and keeps its original value 4.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code:
unsigned char data[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
memset(data, 0, 3);

questions.prompt: Does zeroing a five-byte array make reading data[5] safe? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Valid element indices are 0 through 4; data[5] is outside the array regardless of its initialization.
questions.hint: Initialization changes values, not object boundaries.
questions.explanation: Bounds must be checked against the actual buffer and received stream length. memset does not enlarge either.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1. Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Rejects reading data[5].
States the valid indices and separates bounds from initialization.

questions.prompt: A decoder clears its buffer, then reads a last byte 0x0f whose low four bits are padding. Are those received padding bits now zero? How should the decoder handle them?
questions.answer: No. Reading 0x0f overwrites the cleared byte, including its low bits. Follow the field lengths and stopping rules, ignoring padding as specified.
questions.hint: The input store happens after the clearing operation.
questions.explanation: Pre-zeroing cannot erase bits written afterward. For Problem 1, unused trailing bits are ignored; Problem 2 uses its stated termination rules.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples. Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples. Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
rubric: Says received padding can still contain ones.
Uses protocol boundaries rather than assuming zero padding.

questions.prompt: Which single C operator performs bit-by-bit AND: & or &&?
questions.hint: One combines bit positions; the other tests truth.
questions.explanation: & keeps a bit set only where both operands have that bit set. && instead returns 0 or 1 from the operands’ truth values.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does x receive?
questions.hint: Compare the one-bits at corresponding positions.
questions.explanation: 2u is binary 10 and 1u is binary 01, so their bitwise AND is 00. Using && here would instead produce 1.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
questions.code: unsigned int x = 2u & 1u;

questions.prompt: Write an unsigned expression with exactly bit k set, where 0 <= k < 32 and bit 0 is the least significant bit.
questions.answer: 1u << k
questions.hint: Start with one at bit 0 and move it k places.
questions.explanation: The u suffix makes the left operand unsigned int. The stated shift-count range avoids an invalid shift.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Uses a value with exactly one initial set bit.
Shifts it left by k using an unsigned operand.

questions.prompt: What is the decimal value of the mask `1u << 5`?
questions.hint: Bit k has weight 2^k.
questions.explanation: Moving the unsigned one five places left yields binary 100000, which is 32.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: Write a statement that sets bit k of unsigned int x to 1 and preserves all other bits. Assume 0 <= k < 32.
questions.hint: OR with a mask whose only one-bit is at k.
questions.explanation: OR with 1 sets that bit; OR with 0 leaves every other bit unchanged.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Builds an unsigned one-bit mask at k.
Uses OR, preserving all other bits.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in x after the operation?
questions.hint: Only bit 1 is forced to one.
questions.explanation: 8u is 1000; the mask is 0010. Their OR is 1010, or 10.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
questions.code:
unsigned int x = 8u;
x |= 1u << 1;

questions.prompt: Write a statement that clears bit k of unsigned int x and preserves all other bits. Assume 0 <= k < 32.
questions.hint: Invert a one-bit mask, then combine with AND.
questions.explanation: The inverted mask has a zero at k and ones elsewhere. AND clears only the selected bit.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Uses an inverted unsigned one-bit mask.
Uses AND to preserve all other bits.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in x afterward?
questions.hint: 15 is binary 1111; clear the bit of weight 4.
questions.explanation: The mask clears bit 2, turning 1111 into 1011, which is 11.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
questions.code:
unsigned int x = 15u;
x &= ~(1u << 2);

questions.prompt: Write a statement that toggles bit k of unsigned int x while preserving the others. Assume 0 <= k < 32.
questions.hint: XOR with one flips a bit.
questions.explanation: XOR with the one-bit mask flips bit k; XOR with zero leaves the remaining bits unchanged.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Uses XOR.
Applies an unsigned mask containing only bit k.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does x have after both statements?
questions.hint: Toggling the same bit twice restores it.
questions.explanation: The first XOR flips bit 1 off; the second flips it back on. The final value equals the original 10.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `40u >> 3`?
questions.hint: Unsigned right shift divides by powers of two, discarding low bits.
questions.explanation: 40 divided by 8 is 5. For unsigned values, right shift introduces zeros on the left.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `43u >> 3`?
questions.hint: Discard the low three bits.
questions.explanation: 43 / 8 has integer quotient 5. The three low bits do not round the result upward.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `3u << 2`?
questions.hint: Two left shifts multiply this value by four.
questions.explanation: Binary 0011 becomes 1100. No high bits are lost in this example.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `0x80000000u << 1` under the practice assumptions?
questions.hint: Unsigned results wrap modulo 2^32.
questions.explanation: The only set bit moves beyond the 32-bit unsigned width and is discarded. This unsigned operation is defined.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: Classify `1u << 32` with a 32-bit unsigned int. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.answer: undefined
questions.hint: A shift count must be smaller than the promoted left operand’s width.
questions.explanation: A count equal to 32 is invalid for a 32-bit operand. Unsigned arithmetic does not make an out-of-range shift count valid.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: Classify `1u >> -1`. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.answer: undefined
questions.hint: Check the shift count before the direction.
questions.explanation: A negative shift count causes undefined behavior, including for unsigned operands.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: Classify `1 << 31` when int is 32 bits. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.answer: undefined
questions.hint: The literal 1 has type int, not unsigned int.
questions.explanation: The mathematical result 2^31 is not representable in signed 32-bit int. Use an appropriate unsigned or wider signed operand for the intended operation.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: Which suffix makes the left operand unsigned int in `1___ << 31`? Give just the suffix.
questions.answer: u
questions.hint: The fix is a type choice, not parentheses.
questions.explanation: 1u is unsigned int, making this 31-place shift valid under the 32-bit unsigned assumptions. This does not by itself make unsigned subtraction a signed-decoding formula.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.

questions.prompt: In `data[i] >> shift`, data[i] is unsigned char and 0 <= shift <= 7. Is its promoted value ever negative under the practice assumptions? Explain.
questions.answer: No. unsigned char values are 0..255, all representable in 32-bit int, so promotion to int preserves a nonnegative value.
questions.hint: Small integer operands undergo integer promotion before shifting.
questions.explanation: Using unsigned-char storage avoids signed-char negative byte values. Right shift of these promoted nonnegative values has the intended bit-extraction result.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: States the 0..255 range.
Explains promotion to int preserves that nonnegative value.

questions.prompt: Why does this decoder prefer unsigned char over plain char for input bytes?
questions.answer: unsigned char guarantees values 0..255 in this practice model; plain char may be signed, so bytes with the top bit set can promote to negative int values.
questions.hint: The signedness of plain char is implementation-defined.
questions.explanation: For a negative signed value, right-shift behavior in C17 is implementation-defined. unsigned-char byte storage avoids that complication.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Identifies plain char’s possible signedness.
Connects unsigned-char values to predictable nonnegative shift operands.

questions.prompt: At global stream bit position p = 19, what byte index contains the bit?
questions.hint: Each byte holds eight consecutive stream positions.
questions.explanation: Integer division gives 19 / 8 = 2. The valid positions in byte 2 are 16 through 23.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: A bit is at global position p = 8. What is its byte index?
questions.hint: The first byte ends at global position 7.
questions.explanation: 8 / 8 = 1: position 8 is the first bit of the second byte, not another bit of byte 0.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: For p = 19, how many positions must data[p / 8] shift right to bring the requested bit to bit 0?
questions.hint: Within-byte stream offset is p % 8; reading is MSB first.
questions.explanation: The offset is 3, so the shift is 7 − 3 = 4.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: For p = 8, what right-shift count brings that stream bit to bit 0?
questions.hint: Position 8 begins a new byte.
questions.explanation: p % 8 is 0; the first stream bit in a byte is its most significant bit, so shift by 7.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Write an expression that yields 0 or 1 for global bit p in unsigned-char buffer data. Assume p is valid.
questions.hint: Select the byte, shift the desired bit down, then isolate it.
questions.explanation: p / 8 chooses the byte. MSB-first indexing gives shift 7 − p % 8. & 1u removes every other bit.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.
rubric: Uses p / 8 to select the byte.
Uses 7 − p % 8 for the shift.
Masks with 1 to produce exactly 0 or 1.

questions.prompt: What bit value does this expression yield?
questions.hint: p = 7 selects the last bit of the first byte.
questions.explanation: 0x81 is binary 10000001. Position 7 uses shift 0; masking its low bit produces 1.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: For data = {0x80, 0x01}, what is the value of global bit 8?
questions.hint: Global bit 8 is the MSB of data[1].
questions.explanation: data[1] is 00000001, whose most significant bit is 0. Its one-bit is at global position 15.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: For data = {0x80, 0x01}, what is the value of global bit 15?
questions.hint: Global bit 15 is the final bit of the second byte.
questions.explanation: 15 / 8 = 1 and 7 − 15 % 8 = 0. The low bit of 0x01 is 1.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: A buffer holds B = 5 bytes. What is the last valid global bit position?
questions.hint: Positions begin at zero.
questions.explanation: There are 8 × 5 = 40 bits, so positions run from 0 through 39.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: B = 2. What is the first out-of-range global bit position?
questions.hint: The first invalid position equals the bit count.
questions.explanation: Two bytes contain positions 0 through 15. Position 16 would access data[2], beyond this buffer.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: The next bit b is 0 or 1. Write the update that appends b on the right of unsigned accumulator value.
questions.answer: value = (value << 1) | b;
questions.hint: Make one low-bit space before inserting b.
questions.explanation: Left shift moves the existing bits up one place; OR inserts b at the new least significant position. Addition of b is also equivalent here.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.
rubric: Shifts the previous value left by one.
Inserts b in the vacated low position.

questions.prompt: value is 5 and the next bit b is 1. What is the new value after `(value << 1) | b`?
questions.hint: Old binary 101 becomes 1011.
questions.explanation: The update is 2 × 5 + 1 = 11. It preserves the order of bits encountered.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Starting from zero, accumulate bits 1, 0, 1, 1 in that order using left-shift-and-append. What decimal value results?
questions.hint: The first received bit becomes the most significant bit of this four-bit field.
questions.explanation: The intermediate values are 1, 2, 5, 11. Do not reverse the received bit order.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Starting from zero, accumulate the five header bits 0, 1, 0, 0, 0. What unsigned L results?
questions.hint: Treat the header as the binary number 01000.
questions.explanation: The accumulator evolves 0, 1, 2, 4, 8. This header requests an 8-bit payload.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: data is {0x12, 0x34}. Read 8 bits beginning at global position 4, MSB first. What unsigned decimal value results?
questions.hint: Join the low four bits of 0x12 to the high four bits of 0x34.
questions.explanation: The selected bits are 0010 0011, which is 0x23 = 35. The field crosses a byte boundary without resetting its accumulator.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: data is {0xab, 0xcd}. Read 6 bits beginning at global position 6. What unsigned decimal value results?
questions.hint: Take the last two bits of 0xab, then the first four bits of 0xcd.
questions.explanation: The selected bits are 11 followed by 1100: 111100 = 60.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: A field’s header begins at global position 13. At what position does its payload begin?
questions.hint: The header is always five bits.
questions.explanation: The payload starts at headerStart + 5 = 18. It does not start at the next byte boundary.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: A header starts at position 6 and announces L = 9. At what position would the next field’s header begin?
questions.hint: Advance across both the five-bit header and the payload.
questions.explanation: The next position is 6 + 5 + 9 = 20. Fields can begin anywhere within a byte.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: What is the largest unsigned raw value obtainable from 4 payload bits?
questions.hint: All four raw bits can be one before signed interpretation.
questions.explanation: The raw bit pattern 1111 has unsigned value 15. Its later signed interpretation at L = 4 would be −1.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: What is the largest unsigned raw value obtainable from 31 bits?
questions.hint: Compute 2^31 − 1.
questions.explanation: An unsigned 32-bit accumulator can hold every allowed 31-bit raw payload. Accumulating an arbitrarily long entire Problem 2 stream into one integer is a separate problem.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: For a payload of length L = 6, what bit index in raw is its sign bit? Use LSB-based bit numbering.
questions.hint: The highest of L bits has index L − 1.
questions.explanation: The sign bit is bit 5 of this six-bit raw field, not bit 31 of its storage type.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: Write an unsigned expression that tests whether an L-bit raw payload is negative. Assume 1 <= L <= 31.
questions.hint: The payload’s own most significant bit carries its sign.
questions.explanation: A shifted-and-masked alternative is also valid. Test bit L − 1 rather than the storage type’s top bit.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions. Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Selects bit L − 1.
Distinguishes zero from a set sign bit.
Uses a safe shift for the stated L range.

questions.prompt: The L = 4 payload is 1101 (unsigned raw = 13). What signed value does it encode?
questions.hint: With its sign bit set, subtract 2^L.
questions.explanation: 13 − 16 = −3. The header is not included in this signed conversion.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: The L = 5 payload is 11111 (unsigned raw = 31). What signed value does it encode?
questions.hint: Subtract the modulus for this payload width.
questions.explanation: 31 − 32 = −1. All ones encodes −1 at every nonzero two’s-complement width.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: For L = 4 and raw = 0, what signed value is decoded?
questions.hint: A zero sign bit means nonnegative, not strictly positive.
questions.explanation: The sign bit is clear, so keep raw unchanged. Zero is a valid integer payload, distinct from a zero length header.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: For L = 5 and raw = 15 (01111), what signed value is decoded?
questions.hint: Only the highest of these five bits determines negativity.
questions.explanation: The sign bit at index 4 is zero, so the signed value remains 15.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum value representable by an L = 5 two’s-complement payload?
questions.hint: An L-bit signed range begins at −2^(L−1).
questions.explanation: The minimum bit pattern is 10000, raw 16. Subtracting 32 gives −16.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum value representable by an L = 31 two’s-complement payload?
questions.hint: Use the payload width, not the 32-bit storage width.
questions.explanation: The minimum is −2^30 = −1073741824. The PDF’s −1073741823 example is close to, but is not, that minimum.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: A one-bit payload is 1. What signed value does it encode?
questions.hint: Its only bit is also its sign bit.
questions.explanation: raw = 1 and L = 1, so 1 − 2 = −1. A one-bit signed field cannot encode positive 1.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: What is the largest signed value representable by a one-bit payload?
questions.hint: The two available patterns encode zero and negative one.
questions.explanation: Pattern 0 encodes 0 and pattern 1 encodes −1; therefore the maximum is 0.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.

questions.prompt: Repair the negative branch so it is defined even when L = 31. raw is unsigned int and contains at most L bits.
questions.answer: return (int)((long long)raw - (1LL << L));
questions.hint: Do the power of two and subtraction in a signed type wide enough for 2^31.
questions.explanation: 1 << 31 is invalid for signed 32-bit int. long long safely holds raw, 2^L and their difference; the final result fits int under these assumptions.
questions.source: WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31. Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
questions.code:
/* sign bit is known to be set */
return (int)raw - (1 << L);
rubric: Uses a type wide enough for 2^31, such as long long.
Subtracts 2^L from raw with signed wide arithmetic.
Produces the signed int result without relying on an out-of-range unsigned-to-int conversion.

questions.prompt: Why is `return raw - (1u << L);` not a portable substitute for the negative branch of an int-returning decoder? Give a safe expression.
questions.answer: The subtraction is unsigned, so a negative mathematical answer wraps to a large unsigned value; converting that out-of-range value to int is implementation-defined in C17. Use (int)((long long)raw - (1LL << L)).
questions.hint: Changing the shift operand to unsigned also changes the subtraction’s arithmetic type.
questions.explanation: An unsigned mask is useful for bit tests. Signed interpretation needs arithmetic whose negative result is representable before the final conversion.
questions.source: WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31. Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Identifies unsigned subtraction and wraparound.
Avoids assuming out-of-range unsigned-to-int conversion is portable.
Gives a safe wider signed subtraction.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum value representable by an L = 31 two’s-complement payload?
questions.hint: The sign bit must stay zero; the other 30 bits may all be one.
questions.explanation: The maximum is 2^30 − 1 = 1073741823. A 31-bit signed payload has one sign bit and 30 remaining bits; do not use the 32-bit int maximum.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload and positive extreme example; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s assumptions.

questions.prompt: In Problem 2, what is the minimum number of remaining bits required to attempt another encoded integer?
questions.hint: Five header bits plus at least one payload bit.
questions.explanation: With 5 or fewer remaining bits, the assignment says stop. Six bits can hold a width-1 field.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: There are exactly 5 bits left in a Problem 2 stream. Should the decoder continue or stop?
questions.answer: stop
questions.hint: The stopping rule includes equality at five.
questions.explanation: Even a full five-bit length header would leave no bit for a nonzero-length payload.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: After reading a header, pos points to its payload. Write a safe condition that confirms L payload bits remain, assuming pos <= totalBits.
questions.answer: L <= totalBits - pos
questions.hint: Use the remaining count rather than unchecked addition.
questions.explanation: Comparing against totalBits − pos avoids overflow in pos + L. This is a defensive buffer check in addition to the assignment’s termination rules.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples. Supporting C: size_t bounds arithmetic.
rubric: Compares L with the available payload bits.
Uses the stated pos <= totalBits precondition.

questions.prompt: totalBits = 16 and pos = 10 after reading a header. L = 7. How many payload bits are actually available?
questions.hint: Subtract the current cursor from the total.
questions.explanation: Only 16 − 10 = 6 bits remain, so a 7-bit read would exceed the buffer. A robust helper rejects it rather than inventing missing bits.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples. Supporting C: array bounds.

questions.prompt: pos is 7 at the start of a field and L = 4. After consuming its header and payload, what is pos?
questions.hint: Advance once for five header bits and once for L payload bits.
questions.explanation: 7 + 5 + 4 = 16. Do not add an extra byte-alignment step.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: pos is 12 immediately after the header. L = 3. After consuming the payload, what is pos?
questions.hint: The question starts after the header has already been consumed.
questions.explanation: Only L remains to be added: 12 + 3 = 15. Adding the header again would skip stream bits.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: A Problem 2 length header decodes to L = 0. Should the decoder print zero or stop? Answer print or stop.
questions.answer: stop
questions.hint: Length zero is a control value, not a zero-valued payload.
questions.explanation: A zero length terminates decoding that bitstream. Numeric zero is encoded using a nonzero L and an all-zero payload.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: A stream has already produced two integers and then encounters L = 0. How many additional integer output lines does that header produce?
questions.hint: A terminator does not receive an integer ordinal.
questions.explanation: Stop without printing another integer or incrementing the successful-integer counter.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: The previous input line produced four integers. What ordinal is used for the first decoded integer on the next input line?
questions.hint: The integer counter belongs to one input bitstream.
questions.explanation: Reset the ordinal to 1 for each input line; line numbering and integer numbering are separate counters.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.

questions.prompt: At the start of each input line, what happens to pos and ordinal? What advances when a B = 0 line produces no integers?
questions.answer: Reset pos to 0 and ordinal to 1 for the new line. The input line number still advances; no integer is printed.
questions.hint: Separate byte-stream state from the outer line counter.
questions.explanation: pos and ordinal are local to one bitstream. Empty lines do not collapse the input’s line numbering.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples. Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.
rubric: Resets the stream cursor and integer ordinal for each line.
Advances input line number even when nothing is printed.

questions.prompt: Problem 1 receives the one-byte stream 0x08. What signed integer should be printed?
questions.hint: Write 0x08 as eight bits, then split 5 header bits from the payload.
questions.explanation: 00001000 begins with L = 00001 = 1, followed by payload 0. The remaining two bits are ignored.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Problem 1 receives the one-byte stream 0x0c. What signed integer should be printed?
questions.hint: The header still has five bits; the one payload bit is now set.
questions.explanation: 00001100 splits into header 00001 and payload 1. A one-bit signed 1 means −1; the final two bits are padding.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Problem 1 receives the one-byte stream 0x12. What signed integer should be printed?
questions.hint: Split 00010010 after its first five bits.
questions.explanation: The header 00010 gives L = 2. The payload 01 has a clear sign bit and encodes +1; one trailing bit is ignored.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Problem 1 receives bytes {0x43, 0xd8}. What signed integer is decoded?
questions.hint: The header is 01000; read the next eight bits across the byte boundary.
questions.explanation: L = 8 and the payload is 01111011, raw 123. Its sign bit is zero; the last three bits are ignored.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Problem 1 receives {0xca, 0xf1, 0x85, 0x38}. What signed integer is decoded?
questions.hint: The five-bit header is 11001; the 25-bit payload is positive.
questions.explanation: L = 25; the next 25 bits have raw value 12345678 and sign bit zero. The PDF sample’s expected value is 12345678.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.

questions.prompt: Decode Problem 2 bytes {0x08, 0x30}. Give the signed values in order and the cursor position after each integer.
questions.answer: Values: 0, -1. Cursor positions: 6, 12. Four bits remain, so stop.
questions.hint: Each of these fields uses a five-bit header and one payload bit.
questions.explanation: The first six bits are 00001|0; the next six are 00001|1. Ordinals are 1 and 2 on the same input line.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.
rubric: Gives values 0 then −1.
Gives positions 6 and 12.
Stops with 4 remaining bits.

questions.prompt: Decode Problem 2 bytes {0x12, 0x28, 0x6c, 0x70}. Give the four signed values in order and the final cursor.
questions.answer: Values: 1, -2, 3, -4. Final cursor: 30; two bits remain.
questions.hint: Read each new length at the current bit cursor, not at the next byte.
questions.explanation: The payload widths are 2, 2, 3, 3; field sizes are 7, 7, 8, 8. These sum to 30 bits.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples.
rubric: Gives 1, −2, 3, −4 in order.
Gives final cursor 30.
Stops because only 2 bits remain.

questions.prompt: A decoder allocates 16 bytes but successfully reads B = 2 bytes. Should totalBits be 128 or 16? Explain which length controls decoding.
questions.answer: totalBits is 16, from the two received bytes. Allocated capacity is not the length of the received stream.
questions.hint: Storage space and valid input length are different quantities.
questions.explanation: Decoding unused allocation would interpret unrelated bytes as part of the input. Use B for the valid stream length and separately ensure capacity is at least B.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples. Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
rubric: Uses 8 × B = 16 bits.
Distinguishes allocated capacity from received byte count.

questions.prompt: A 10-byte allocation contains only B = 3 successfully received input bytes. What is the first global bit position that is outside this received stream?
questions.hint: Use received bytes, not allocated capacity, to set the stream boundary.
questions.explanation: The received stream contains 3 × 8 = 24 bits at positions 0 through 23. The extra allocation does not extend the input stream.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: B gives the received byte count; supporting C: allocation capacity and initialized input length are separate.

questions.prompt: Write getBit from memory. Contract: data points to a valid byte buffer; p is a valid global bit position; return exactly 0 or 1 in MSB-first stream order.
questions.hint: Recall the three steps: select byte, move bit, isolate bit.
questions.explanation: This helper assumes its caller has checked bounds. Its index calculation follows the assignment’s explicit stream order.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples. WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31.
rubric: Uses the requested signature and returns 0 or 1.
Selects data[p / 8].
Shifts by 7 − p % 8 and masks one bit.

questions.prompt: Write getBitChecked. Return 1 on success and store the requested bit in *out; return 0 if p is outside B bytes and leave *out unchanged. Assume data and out are valid for their uses and B <= SIZE_MAX / 8.
questions.hint: Check the position before touching data or the output.
questions.explanation: The boundary is exclusive: p equal to the bit count is already invalid. Checking p / 8 >= B is another valid approach that avoids multiplication.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples. Supporting C for A2 buffers: C17 array, pointer and sizeof rules; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.2.1, 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2, 6.5.3.4, 6.7.6.3.
rubric: Rejects all out-of-range positions before reading.
Leaves *out unchanged on failure.
Stores the correctly extracted 0/1 bit and returns 1 on success.

questions.prompt: Write getBits from memory using getBit. Contract: 0 <= k <= 31; all k requested positions are valid; read from p in increasing stream order. Return the unsigned field, with k = 0 returning 0.
questions.hint: Initialize, repeat exactly k times, append the next bit.
questions.explanation: The loop invariant is that value contains exactly the bits already consumed in their original order. The 31-bit limit keeps the accumulator within unsigned int.
questions.source: WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31.
rubric: Initializes the accumulator to zero.
Consumes exactly p through p + k − 1 in order.
Uses left-shift-and-append and returns the accumulator.
Handles k = 0 without reading a bit.

questions.prompt: Write readField using getBits. Return 1 and write *out when 0 <= k <= 31 and the entire field [p, p+k) fits in totalBits. Otherwise return 0 and leave *out unchanged. All pointers are valid for their uses.
questions.hint: Check p before subtracting it; do not rely on p + k staying in range.
questions.explanation: The ordered bounds checks prevent unsigned subtraction underflow and addition overflow. A zero-length field at p == totalBits is permitted by this helper’s contract.
questions.source: WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31. Supporting C: unsigned bounds arithmetic.
rubric: Rejects k > 31 and p > totalBits.
Checks remaining capacity without unsafe subtraction or addition.
Only writes *out on success.
Accepts a valid zero-bit request and returns zero through *out.

questions.prompt: Write decodeSigned. Contract: 1 <= L <= 31 and raw contains exactly the low L bits of a field. Return its L-bit two’s-complement value without undefined shifts or out-of-range unsigned-to-int conversion.
questions.hint: Test bit L − 1, then subtract 2^L in a sufficiently wide signed type if set.
questions.explanation: The nonnegative branch fits int. The negative branch’s long-long calculation fits and produces a result within the allowed signed payload range.
questions.source: WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31. Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: L-bit signed payload; supporting two’s-complement arithmetic under this practice set’s representation assumptions.
rubric: Tests the payload sign bit at L − 1.
Keeps nonnegative raw values unchanged.
Computes raw − 2^L safely for the negative branch, including L = 31.

questions.prompt: Write readByte. Read one hex integer from stdin. Return 1 and store it in *out only if conversion succeeds and its value is at most 255; otherwise return 0 and leave *out unchanged. Assume the token, if numeric, fits unsigned int.
questions.hint: Match scanf’s destination type before checking the byte range.
questions.explanation: A conversion check prevents use of an unassigned temporary. The range check prevents accepting a value that would be truncated to fit one byte.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 input/output: C17 scanf/printf rules; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2. Assignment 2 PDF, p. 2: input, bit order, Problem 1 processing and examples.
rubric: Uses unsigned int temporary and %x with its address.
Checks both conversion success and the byte range.
Writes through out only after both checks and returns the specified status.

questions.prompt: Write nextValue using getBits and decodeSigned. Status: 1 = decoded one integer; 0 = stop (fewer than 6 bits remain or L == 0); -1 = invalid cursor or incomplete payload. On status 1, update *pos to after the field and set *out. Otherwise leave both unchanged. Assume data holds totalBits valid bits and pointer arguments are valid.
questions.hint: Use a local cursor until every check succeeds; then commit the output and cursor together.
questions.explanation: The five-bit header bounds L at 31. Remaining-capacity checks make both additions safe. Leaving the cursor unchanged on stop/error is this helper’s chosen contract, not an extra rule imposed by the assignment.
questions.source: Assignment 2 PDF, p. 3: Problem 2 encoding, stopping rules and examples. WALKTHROUGH.md, §§3–4: bit-by-bit helpers, with corrected wide signed subtraction at L = 31.
rubric: Checks cursor validity and the fewer-than-six stopping rule before reading.
Reads the five-bit header and stops on zero length.
Rejects an incomplete payload before extraction.
On success decodes the signed value and advances by 5 + L.
Preserves pos and out on stop/error.

questions.prompt: Write lowMask. Contract: 0 <= k <= 31. Return an unsigned int whose low k bits are 1 and remaining bits are 0. Do not loop; support k = 0.
questions.hint: A one at bit k minus one fills every lower bit.
questions.explanation: For k = 0 the expression is 1 − 1 = 0. For k = 31 the unsigned shift is valid. Extending this unchanged to k = 32 would violate the shift-count rule.
questions.source: Supporting C for A2 bit operations: C17 integer promotions, shifts and bitwise operators; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12.
rubric: Uses unsigned arithmetic.
Produces exactly the low k one-bits.
Returns zero for k = 0 and remains defined at k = 31.
